title: On-device Visual Perception for Light-weight Browser Agents
department: Department of Space / Indian Space Research Organisation
dataset_link: Any open-source data can be used. Use cases for evaluation will provided during finale
description:
Background AI agents are becoming omnipresent in the current era and can play an important role in our digital interactions. If an agentic AI pipeline has access to our visual context, screen states, they can assist users in complex workflows and automate many tasks. Most of the agentic AI pipelines are deployed on server side which limits the type to data that a user can share with it. It would open a new dimension of possibilities, if a local agent is deployed on user machine particularly browser which can eliminate the need to share the sensitive data with the server. Local system generally has fewer resources than server and is unable to host a full-fledged pipeline therefore only the non-sensitive data such as structure of the screen, application fields etc can be sent to server for processing.
Modern browser APIs (such as WebGPU and WebAssembly) and local inference libraries (like ONNX Runtime Web and Transformers.js) have unlocked the ability to run lightweight machine learning models directly on the client. The aim is to bridge these two environments: leveraging the reasoning power of cloud or server based AI while strictly enforcing data privacy at the client side.
Description Participants are required to build a privacy-preserving vision agent which runs on browser. This involves implementing a client-side architecture where a local Vision Transformer (ViT) or equivalent computer vision model 'reads' the user's screen and takes decision based on that. If it requires the visual context to be sent to server, it shall sanitize the sensitive/PII data using DOM tags or any other method, before any network request is made. It should dynamically detect and redact sensitive elements. For example, blurring faces, blacking out passwords, and masking PII etc. Only this anonymized, unidentifiable data should be transmitted to the central server which should be aware for this redaction scheme and can process data accordingly. The server will then process the sanitized context and return actionable commands for the browser agent to execute. Participants must balance the trade-offs between inference latency and the accuracy.
Expected Solution A successful submission should include a working prototype consisting of client side extension and server that demonstrates the following:
Client-side (extension/JS) running in popular browsers (chrome, Firefox) components:
• Local Vision Processing: Implementation of a client-side vision model running in the browser (e.g., via WebGPU) that evaluates the current screen state.
• Privacy Preserving Filter: A mechanism for sanitizing sensitive or personal visual data. This can be achieved through local bounding-box redaction, semantic obfuscation, masking etc. This should be clearly demonstrated.
Server-side implementation components:
• Server Side Integration: The transmission of the anonymized visual context to a centralized LLM/VLM, which successfully interprets the sanitized data and returns the response which may be processed data to be again ingested by local client or an UI action (e.g., 'click the submit button,' 'scroll down') that the local client executes.
• Participants are free to use any offline deployable (open-source/open-weights) model on server side. During SIH they can use cloud hosted version of these. An end-to-end task assisting the user should be demonstrated.
Evaluation will be done on the following metrics:
1-Accuracy of visual context from screen – 25% 2-Recall and precision for detection of sensitive/PII data – 20% 3-Precision of redaction – 20% 4-Client side resource utilization – 20% 5-Overall end-to-end latency of the provided task -15%
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, machine learning, computer vision applied to a miscellaneous problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Miscellaneous. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on integration, model, architecture. Sustainability (4/5): has a clear long-term maintenance path. Scalability (3/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 22/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: On-device Visual Perception for Light-weight Browser Agents

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a browser-based AI agent that can understand what's on your screen, structure, buttons, forms, entirely on your own device using lightweight local models, sending only non-sensitive structural information to the cloud, so your actual sensitive screen content never leaves your machine.
overview.why_it_matters: Server-side AI agents need to see your full screen content, a real privacy problem. A genuine local-first architecture lets AI agents assist with complex workflows while keeping sensitive data strictly on-device.
pain_points: Server-side agentic AI pipelines require sharing full visual/screen context, a real privacy concern.
Local devices have far fewer resources than servers, can't host a full agentic pipeline.
No established browser-based architecture correctly splits sensitive local processing from non-sensitive cloud-sendable data.
overview.background: AI agents benefit from visual/screen context, but server-side deployment requires sharing potentially sensitive data, while modern browser technologies (WebGPU, WebAssembly, ONNX Runtime Web) now enable genuinely local, lightweight inference.
overview.whats_being_asked: An on-device visual perception system for browser-based AI agents, running lightweight models locally to understand screen structure/state while strictly keeping sensitive visual data client-side.
expected_solution: On-device (browser-based) visual perception using WebGPU/WebAssembly/ONNX Runtime Web or similar.
Screen structure extraction (elements, fields, layout) without exposing raw sensitive content.
Clear separation between locally-processed sensitive data and non-sensitive data safe to send to a server for further reasoning.
Genuinely lightweight, performant on typical consumer hardware.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. Genuine on-device, browser-native visual perception for agentic AI with a deliberate privacy-preserving architecture is real, cutting-edge, valuable technical territory.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires real browser ML deployment expertise (WebGPU/WASM, model quantization for browser inference) plus genuine architectural design for the privacy-preserving data split.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires genuine on-device ML deployment expertise specifically for browser environments, a narrow, cutting-edge field.

innovation.note: Genuine on-device, privacy-preserving browser AI agent perception is real, cutting-edge, differentiated technical territory.

invention.note: Browser-native ML deployment (WebGPU/WASM) plus genuine privacy-architecture design is substantial technical depth.

technical_feasibility.note: ONNX Runtime Web, Transformers.js, and WebGPU provide real, usable tooling foundations, meaningfully de-risking the build.

impact_and_benefits.note: Genuinely valuable for privacy-preserving AI agent architectures as agentic AI becomes more prevalent.

architecture.note: On-device model inference plus a genuine data-classification/routing layer, real architectural sophistication in the privacy-split design specifically.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, one of the higher-scoring PS in this batch, genuinely achievable using established browser-ML tooling (ONNX Runtime Web, Transformers.js). The real differentiator is your privacy-preserving data-split design, not just running a model in the browser.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Established browser-native ML tooling (ONNX Runtime Web, Transformers.js, WebGPU) provides real, usable technical foundations, this is genuinely achievable, not purely aspirational.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Building on-device inference without a genuine, deliberate architectural design for what counts as 'sensitive' (kept local) versus 'non-sensitive' (sendable to server) would miss the actual privacy-preservation point of this PS.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Design your data-classification/routing logic explicitly and defensibly, clearly define what screen information is genuinely non-sensitive (structural metadata) versus sensitive (actual content), and validate that your split genuinely protects sensitive information from ever leaving the device.

idea_0_4: Choose your on-device ML tooling (ONNX Runtime Web or Transformers.js with WebGPU acceleration are established, usable options).
Design your data-classification architecture: what screen information is structural/non-sensitive versus content/sensitive.
Split: one person on the on-device inference pipeline, one on the classification/routing architecture.
prototype_4_22: Build your on-device visual perception model running in the browser (screen structure/element detection).
Build your data-classification logic distinguishing sensitive from non-sensitive extracted information.
Start testing performance on typical consumer hardware, this is a real constraint worth validating early.
integration_22_30: Connect on-device perception, classification, and a demonstrated (simulated) server-side reasoning step using only the non-sensitive data.
Test with a genuinely sensitive-content scenario (e.g. a form with personal data) to confirm sensitive content never leaves the device.
Measure and optimize on-device inference latency for genuine usability.
polish_30_36: Build a clear demo showing local processing happening entirely in-browser, with only non-sensitive structural data visibly sent onward.
Rehearse a live demo, ideally showing network traffic (or lack thereof) to prove sensitive content genuinely stays local.
Prepare to discuss your specific sensitive/non-sensitive classification design decisions.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show, live, that sensitive on-screen content (like a filled form field) is processed entirely locally and never appears in any network traffic sent to a server, monitor and display network calls during the demo if possible, that visible, verifiable privacy guarantee is the concrete proof this PS's core value proposition depends on.

strengths: Established browser-native ML tooling provides real, usable technical foundations.
Genuine, timely privacy-relevance as agentic AI becomes more prevalent.
weaknesses: Genuine on-device performance on typical consumer hardware needs real optimization and validation.
The sensitive/non-sensitive data classification design requires careful, defensible thought, not an arbitrary split.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Browser-ML-skill-weighted, with real, deliberate design thought on the privacy-classification architecture.
team_fit.approach: Get basic on-device inference working early using established tooling, then invest remaining time in the genuine privacy-architecture design and validation.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: The on-device model inference pipeline using established browser-ML frameworks.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Designing a genuinely defensible sensitive/non-sensitive data classification architecture, that's a real privacy-engineering design decision requiring careful thought, not a default split.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded system without deliberate, carefully-designed data classification could accidentally leak genuinely sensitive information to the server side, undermining the entire privacy-preservation premise of this PS.

data_resource_availability.status: No external dataset dependency, this is a browser-ML deployment and architecture-design challenge using your own test web pages/forms.

judge_qna.question: Can you prove sensitive content genuinely never leaves the device, not just that you claim it doesn't?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Demonstrate this live by monitoring network traffic during a test with sensitive on-screen content, showing no sensitive data appears in any outgoing request.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your specific definition of 'sensitive' versus 'non-sensitive' data, and how confident are you it's comprehensive?

judge_qna.question: How does your on-device model perform on typical consumer hardware, not just a high-end development machine?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Present your actual measured inference latency and any performance testing across different hardware capability levels.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your fallback behavior on genuinely resource-constrained devices where local inference is too slow?
